name: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2001.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi constitute a site embracing almost 30 ha of hillside within Kampala district. Most of the site is agricultural, farmed by traditional methods. At its core on the hilltop is the former palace of the Kabakas of Buganda, built in 1882 and converted into the royal burial ground in 1884. Four royal tombs now lie within the Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, the main building, which is circular and surmounted by a dome. It is a major example of an architectural achievement in organic materials, principally wood, thatch, reed, wattle and daub. The site's main significance lies, however, in its intangible values of belief, spirituality, continuity and identity.”

The Kasubi Tombs, in Kampala, are the burial ground of four kabakas, the kings of Buganda, and other members of the royal family. Wikipedia calls the site an important spiritual and political place for the Ganda people.

Major buildings there were almost completely destroyed by fire in March 2010, and the article says the cause was under investigation. The site was put on the List of World Heritage in Danger in July 2010.

Reconstruction began in 2014, funded by a fundraising campaign called Etofaali and by the government of Japan. After the buildings were restored in 2023, the article says, the site was removed from the danger list.

gaps: The Buganda Kingdom's own account of the fire and the rebuilding, and of what the tombs mean today.
